characterList.description: Black woman with glasses wearing a green and brown African dress, a white headscarf and a silver necklace
characterList.name: Leymah Gbowee

content_metadata.description: An interview with Nobel Peace Prize laureate Leymah Gbowee, discussing her work as a peace activist, her thoughts on the challenges faced by women in the field of peace and security, and the 20th anniversary of the UNSC Resolution 1325.

qAndA.answer: Leymah Gbowee is wearing a green and brown dress.
qAndA.question: What color is the dress Leymah Gbowee is wearing?

qAndA.answer: Leymah Gbowee won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011.
qAndA.question: What year did Leymah Gbowee win the Nobel Peace Prize?

qAndA.answer: According to Leymah Gbowee, one obstacle women continue to face is access to funding.
qAndA.question: What is one obstacle that women continue to face in peace building, according to Leymah Gbowee?

qAndA.answer: Leymah Gbowee describes the peace and security field as a male domain where women face patriarchal attitudes.
qAndA.question: How does Leymah Gbowee describe the peace and security field?

qAndA.answer: Leymah Gbowee wishes that the 3 Ps around the Resolution - participation, prevention, and protection - would be taken into consideration and that the Resolution would become an 'adult' and achieve its intended purpose.
qAndA.question: What are Leymah Gbowee's birthday wishes for the UNSC Resolution 1325?

scenes.thematicElements: Peace, Women's Rights, Nobel Peace Prize
scenes.title: Leymah Gbowee's Introduction

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'WHO ARE YOU?'
Text appears on screen: 'My name is Leymah Roberta Gbowee. I am a peace activist, a women's rights advocate and 2011 co-winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.'
Text below 'Leymah Gbowee' appears and disappears gradually: 'PEACE ACTIVIST, NOBEL PEACE PRIZE LAUREATE, LIBERIA

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee is asked about the positive impacts of her work and activism
Leymah Gbowee says that her work had a lot of impact and explains how her activism contributed to the signing of the peace accord in Liberia

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'WHERE DO YOU FEEL THAT YOUR WORK/ACTIVISM HAS OR HAD A POSITIVE IMPACT?

Text appears on screen: 'Well, I think over the years my work has made a lot of impact: Our activism during the civil war in Liberia that contributed to the signing of the peace accord that has led to us enjoying the kind of peace that we enjoy today.'

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee describes her work as an advocate, including her work for the passing of the Resolution around rape and sexual violence in war, and her activism for the protection of women in crisis
Leymah Gbowee mentions that she has also been involved in working with students and mentoring women

scenes.thematicElements: Sexual Violence, Wilton Park, Peace Table, Women in Crisis, Mentoring
scenes.title: Advocacy and Mentorship

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'My work as an advocate for the passing of the Resolution around rape and sexual violence in war, at Wilton Park; My activism about the need for women to be at the Peace Table and my activism about the protection of women in crisis. I feel like over the years, I've made a huge impact. Recently, I've gotten involved in working with students, mentoring women, and the next generation of leaders in Africa and across the world and I also feel like that has made an impact in the world.'

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee is asked about the obstacles she encountered during her career
Leymah Gbowee explains that she doesn't focus on obstacles and that she had to face patriarchal attitudes in the peace and security field
Leymah Gbowee mentions the difficulties women face accessing funding

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'WHAT KIND OF OBSTACLES DID YOU HAVE TO OVERCOME TO ESTABLISH YOURSELF IN YOUR PROFESSIONAL FIELD/FIELD OF ACTIVISM?

Text appears on screen: 'You know, one of the things that I often tell myself: I don't focus on obstacles, because it is all around, especially in peace and security field. It's a field that's seen as male domain, so once you step in, you encounter a lot of patriarchal attitude. So it was there, but I put my feet down, walked through the door boldly and so those obstacles became blocks for me to walk all over to get to where I needed to get to. But one obstacle that women continue to face in the work that we do, is access to funding. This is something that has hampered the great work that women are doing, especially at the grassroots level. It's been there from when I started and it's still there till today.'

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee is asked if there were times in her work where she approached a situation differently than expected

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'DO YOU THINK THAT THERE WERE TIMES IN YOUR WORK/ACTIVISM IN THE FIELD OF PEACE AND SECURITY WHERE YOU APPROACHED A SITUATION DIFFERENTLY THAN EXPECTED?

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee talks about the period after the civil war in Liberia and how different groups came together to start peace
Leymah Gbowee explains that the peace was approached through interfaith, interethnic dialogue and an all-women peace movement
Leymah Gbowee is asked if she has seen a change in the narrative around women, peace and security in the last 20 years
Leymah Gbowee mentions that she has seen a huge change, but that the work needs to be translated into policy and an increase in the number of women at the Peace Table and at leadership level

scenes.thematicElements: Interfaith Dialogue, Interethnic Dialogue, Women's Movement, Policy, Leadership
scenes.title: Post-War Peace Building

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'In 2003 in Liberia, we had gone through a period of war, a protracted period of war, and different groups came together to start peace. But what was interesting about the way we approached peace was through a interfaith, interethnic kind of thing, an all-women peace movement and it made a huge difference.
Text appears on screen: 'DO YOU SEE A CHANGE IN THE NARRATIVE AROUND WOMEN, PEACE AND SECURITY IN THE LAST 20 YEARS?

Text appears on screen: 'Well, over the last 20 years, I've definitely seen a huge change in the narrative around women, peace and security. The narrative that today when we are talking about peace and security, there is always an inclusion of grassroots women and the important work that they are doing at the community levels. What I haven't seen happen is that kind of work translate into policy, the increase of women at the Peace Table, an increase of women at the leadership level in different countries and at the international level.

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee is asked about her birthday wishes for the 20th anniversary of the UNSC Resolution 1325

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'IT'S THE 20TH BIRTHDAY OF UNSC RESOLUTION 1325, ANY BIRTHDAY WISHES?

narrativeProgression.description: Leymah Gbowee says that her birthday wish is that the 3 Ps around the Resolution 1325 (participation, prevention and protection) are taken into consideration
Leymah Gbowee mentions that 1325 has lived for 20 years and is now a 'full woman', meaning that it's time for the Resolution to achieve its intended purpose

videoEditingDetails.description: Text appears on screen: 'Well, that the 3 Ps around the Resolution 1325 would really be taking into consideration: participation, prevention and protection of women. These are the things that I think we still lag behind on. Also to make 1325 live 20 years, she's a full woman and it's time for her to be an adult and to do the good that we brought her into the world to do.
A black background is displayed while a green line crosses the screen from the bottom left to the top right corner and the words 'NO WOMEN/NO PEACE', '20 YEARS UNSC RESOLUTION 1325' appear gradually

climax.description: Leymah Gbowee reflects on the change in the narrative around women, peace, and security over the past 20 years and hopes for its future.

storylines.description: The interview traces Leymah Gbowee's journey as a peace activist, overcoming obstacles, and her reflections on the significance of the UNSC Resolution 1325 after 20 years.

content_metadata.title: Interview with Leymah Gbowee

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: My name is Lema Roberta Bowie. I'm a peace activist of women's rights advocate in 2011
co-winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.
Well I think over the years my work has made a lot of impact. Our activism during the
Civil War in Liberia that contributed to the signing of the Peace Accord that has led to
us enjoying the kind of peace that we enjoy today. My work as an advocate for
the passing of the resolution around rape and sexual violence in war at Wilson Park. My activism
about the need for women to be at the peace table and my activism about the protection of women
in crisis. I feel like over the years I've made a huge impact recently. I've gradually involved
in working with students, mentoring women and the next generation of leaders in Africa and across
the world and I also feel like that has made an impact in the world.
You know one of the things that I often tell myself I don't focus on obstacles because it's all
around especially in the peace and security field. It's a field I've seen as a male domain so once
you step in you encounter a lot of patriarchal attitude so it was there but I put my feet down,
walked through the dough, boldly and so those obstacles became blocks for me to walk all over to
get to where I needed to get to but one obstacle that we may continue to face in the work that we do
is access to funding. This is something that has hampered the great work that women are doing
especially at the grassroots level. It's been there from when I started and it's still there
to date.
In 2003 in light period we had gone through a period of war, a projected period of war and
different groups came together to start peace but what was interesting about it? We were
pushed peace, was through an interfaith, inter-ethnic kind of thing and all women peace movement and it made
a huge difference.
Well over the last 20 years I've definitely seen a huge change in the narrative around women
peace and security, the narrative that today when they're talking about peace and security there's
always an inclusion of grassroots women and the important work that they're doing at the community
levels. What I haven't seen happening is that kind of work translate into policy, the increase
of women at the peace table and the increase of women at the leadership level in different countries
and at the international level.
Well that the three peace around the resolution in 1925 will really be taking into consideration
participation, prevention and protection of women. These are things that I think we still lag behind
on. Also to make 1925 live 20 years she's a full woman and it's time for her to be an adult and
to do the good that we brought her into the world to do.

youtube_description: Leymah Roberta Gbowee is a Liberian peace and women’s rights activist and 2011 co-winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. She was interviewed by the Heinrich Böll Foundation in the context of the project "No Women - No Peace: 20th Anniversary of UNSC Resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security": https://eu.boell.org/en/no-women-no-peace
